summary:
Delaware is a state within the United States, so entry rules, passport and visa policy, and federal identity screening are governed by federal measures rather than Delaware law; the national record carries that layer.

Delaware imposes no ban on transgender people using public bathrooms and facilities according to their gender identity, per the Movement Advancement Project equality map (the archived equality-map URL returned HTTP 404 at the time of checking).

Since 2013 Delaware law prohibits discrimination on the basis of actual or perceived gender identity in employment, housing, public accommodations and other areas under SB 97, which passed the Senate 11-7 on 6 June 2013, passed the House 24-17 with amendments, passed the Senate on amendments 11-9 on 18 June, was signed the next day and took effect immediately.

Since 2013 Delaware imposes additional penalties for a violent crime motivated by the victim's actual or perceived gender identity.

HB142 to formally repeal the common-law gay and trans panic defense and ban its usage was introduced in May 2023 and passed both houses of the Legislature in June 2023, with the Governor yet to either sign or veto it.

Transgender people may change their legal gender on state-issued identification with only the signed statement of a licensed medical provider, and as of 11 February 2017 sex reassignment surgery is no longer an explicit requirement for an amended birth certificate, which instead requires a signed affidavit of surgical, hormonal, psychological or other treatment appropriate for gender transition.

A 2015 law signed 25 June 2015 and effective immediately allows inmates to access and change the name on birth certificates to reflect gender identity, where previously inmates could only change names due to religious beliefs.

Since 26 March 2016 Delaware has prohibited discrimination based on gender identity within insurance contracts, including sex reassignment surgery.

As of April 2020 Delaware does not offer a gender X option on drivers licenses.

An 11 August 2009 executive order protects employees of state executive branch departments and agencies from discrimination on the basis of gender identity.

Since 26 July 2018 (SB 65, signed and effective 23 July 2018 as Laws of Delaware 81:340, introduced 26 April 2017), Delaware defines conversion therapy to include practices seeking to change gender identity, behaviors or gender expressions and makes it unprofessional conduct subject to discipline for physicians, nurses, mental health and chemical dependency professionals, psychologists and clinical social workers to perform it on a minor or refer a minor out-of-state for it, while prohibiting the Department of Services for Children, Youth and Their Families from performing or recommending it for a minor.

A July 2026 national legal risk assessment lists Delaware in its Low-Risk States group (AZ, DE, ME, MI, NV, PA, VA, WI, DC), described as states that largely refrain from targeting transgender adults without specialising in their protection.
tangentialFactors:
Delaware's protections are statutory and executive-order based rather than constitutional, so they rest on the continued willingness of the legislature and governor to maintain them; the pending HB142 shows bills can pass both houses and still await executive action.

Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1 January 1973 following repeal of the sodomy law in July 1972, and since 2009 Delaware law has prohibited discrimination on the basis of actual or perceived sexual orientation in employment, housing, public accommodations and other areas, supplemented by an 11 August 2009 executive order for state executive branch employees.

Civil unions granting the rights, benefits, protections and responsibilities of married persons were available from 1 January 2012, and same-sex marriage was legalized effective 1 July 2013 with conversion of civil unions to marriages.

Since 1 July 2001 Delaware has imposed additional penalties for violent crime motivated by the victim's actual or perceived sexual orientation.

A May 2021 bill passed to repeal a loophole preventing claims based solely on one exclusive sexual orientation awaits the Governor's signature or veto, and HB275 passed 21-15 in the House on 28 March 2024 to include asexuals and pansexuals in the definition of sexual orientation, awaiting a Senate vote.

Since June 2021 a law protects individuals from discrimination based on HIV medicine and PrEP, and in April 2017 the Legislature passed a law allowing HIV patients to donate to other HIV patients, signed and effective 1 January 2018.
localsOnly:
Delaware's own prison system has no documented Delaware-specific placement policy for transgender inmates; the shifts described in national sources (a January 2015 ICE memo directing housing by gender identity, 2016 federal DOJ guidelines forbidding assignment solely on birth anatomy, and a 2018 Federal Bureau of Prisons revision making 'biological sex' the initial determination with gender identity used only 'in rare cases') are federal policies, not Delaware practice.

State executive branch employees and applicants are covered by Executive Order Eight of 11 August 2009, which extended anti-discrimination safeguards to gender identity and reauthorized the Governor's Council on Equal Employment Opportunity with a charge to foster an inclusive environment among executive-branch employees.

In January 2025 Governor Hall-Long signed an Executive Order creating Delaware's LGBTQ+ Commission.
outOfScopeNotes:
The archived Movement Advancement Project equality map URL returned HTTP 404 at the time of checking; the finding of no Delaware bathroom ban rests on the underlying map's recorded data rather than a live page fetch.

HB142's status as of the source's writing is unresolved: it passed both houses in June 2023 with no recorded gubernatorial signature or veto.

Whether HB275 (passed by the House 28 March 2024) cleared the Senate is not sourced here.

No Delaware-specific transgender inmate placement policy is documented in the sources reviewed.
